headline: Drug Used for Diabetes Shows Promise in Slowing Aging Itself
meta_description: NIH-funded research finds semaglutide extended lifespan and reduced aging signs in older mice, opening new possibilities for longevity science.
summary_short: Scientists discover that semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, may slow aging itself—extending lifespan and improving memory and muscle function in o…
body:
In a striking discovery that could reshape how we think about aging, researchers funded by the National Institutes of Health found that semaglutide—the active ingredient in popular diabetes and weight-loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy—extended lifespan by nearly 100 days in older mice while improving memory, muscle function, and blood-sugar control. The UC Berkeley team, led by Danica Chen, treated 20-month-old female mice with the drug for three months and observed improvements in exploratory behavior, spatial memory, and several biological markers of aging, including reduced inflammation and better tissue repair. Most remarkably, the effects went beyond what researchers achieved through calorie restriction alone, suggesting the drug may tap into a separate biological pathway linked to longevity itself.

The key question driving the research was whether semaglutide's benefits simply came from its appetite-suppressing effects. To find out, scientists directly compared the drug against a carefully controlled calorie-restricted diet matched to how much treated mice were eating. While both approaches produced similar results in many areas, semaglutide outperformed calorie restriction in crucial ways: mice on the drug showed better memory and blood-sugar maintenance, and their metabolic rate remained stable rather than slowing down.

"These differences point to the possibility that GLP-1 drugs tap into a biological pathway independent of calorie restriction," Chen said. The implications run deep. If these drugs genuinely influence the aging process itself—rather than simply treating individual diseases—that could explain why they show benefits across such a wide range of health conditions. However, scientists caution that these promising findings in mice don't yet prove the same effects will occur in humans. Additional clinical research, particularly in healthy older adults, will be necessary before we know whether these drugs can meaningfully extend human lifespan.
quick_facts: Semaglutide extended median lifespan nearly 100 days in older mice
UC Berkeley researchers led by Danica Chen conducted the study
Drug improved memory, muscle function, and blood-sugar control
Benefits exceeded those from calorie restriction alone
NIH-funded research published in Nature, September 2026
